question_interpretation: Asks what water supply requirements apply to a dietary supplement manufacturing facility under 21 CFR 111.

issues.detail: 21 CFR 111.16 only requires written procedures for cleaning the physical plant and for pest control; it says nothing about water. The water supply requirements are in 21 CFR 111.15(e), and the related record requirement is in 111.23(c).

J says water that contacts components, product or contact surfaces must be of 'safe and sanitary quality'. In the text, 'safe and sanitary' (plus suitable temperature and pressure) applies to water that does NOT become a component (111.15(e)(1)). Water that may become a component, e.g. water that contacts components, dietary supplements or contact surfaces, must at a minimum comply with applicable Federal, State and local requirements and not contaminate the supplement (111.15(e)(2)).
J leaves out the 111.23(c) records showing that water which may become a component meets 111.15(e)(2), and the plumbing/backflow provisions of 111.15(f) that protect water supplies.

explanation: G names the wrong section. 111.16 is the Subpart C written-procedures section for cleaning and pest control, and the water supply provision is 111.15(e). question_interpretation: Asks whether a dietary supplement manufacturer may rely on a supplier certificate of analysis (COA) instead of its own identity testing of a component.

issues.detail: J says the manufacturer must identity-test a dietary ingredient but leaves out the exception in 111.75(a)(1)(i)-(ii): a firm may petition under 21 CFR 10.30 for an exemption from that testing, and if FDA grants it, alternative testing on FDA's terms applies.

J lists only two COA conditions (qualify the supplier; periodic re-confirmation). It leaves out 111.75(a)(2)(ii)(B), (C) and (E): the COA must describe the test methods, limits and actual results; the firm must document how it qualified the supplier; and QC personnel must review and approve the qualification documentation.

'COA reliance permitted for other component specs only' could be read as barring COA reliance for identity of components that are not dietary ingredients. In fact 111.75(a)(2) lets a qualified COA be used to confirm the identity of those other components as well as their other specifications.

explanation: The core distinction in the key is supported. A dietary ingredient needs at least one identity test or examination by the firm, while other components may be confirmed using a qualified supplier COA. However, the key leaves out the petition-exemption route and three of the five COA reliance conditions, all of which are material to whether reliance is 'allowed'.
proposed_corrected_answer: It depends on the component. For a component that is a dietary ingredient, the firm must conduct at least one appropriate test or examination to verify identity before use, unless it petitions FDA under 21 CFR 10.30 and FDA grants an exemption, in which case it follows FDA's specified alternative testing (111.75(a)(1)). For other components, identity and other 111.70(b) specifications may be confirmed by relying on a supplier COA only if: the firm first qualifies the supplier by confirming the supplier's test results; the COA includes test method description, limits and actual results; the firm documents how it qualified the supplier; it periodically re-confirms the COA; and QC personnel review and approve the qualification documentation (111.75(a)(2)(ii)(A)-(E)). Components stay quarantined until QC reviews and approves results and releases them (111.155(c)).

question_interpretation: Asks who must register a drug establishment, when initial registration is due, and when and how registration is renewed under 21 CFR 207.

issues.detail: The renewal part of the question is governed by 21 CFR 207.29(b): annual review and update between October 1 and December 31, or a certification that nothing changed. G omits 207.29, and 207.29(a) also requires expedited updates within 30 days of certain changes.

J gives no deadlines. Domestic establishments must register within 5 calendar days of beginning operations, and foreign establishments before a drug is imported or offered for import (207.21). J also does not say that the annual update falls in October 1 - December 31.

J's 'manufacturing, preparation, propagation, compounding, or processing' is the statutory wording of FDCA 510, and 207.1 folds those terms into 'manufacture'. Under 207.17(a), however, the registrants are manufacturers, repackers, relabelers and salvagers, domestic and foreign. question_interpretation: Asks what pathogen-reduction performance standard applies to juice under Part 120 and which section sets it.

issues.detail: Recommended enhancement, not a defect: a fuller answer would add four points from 120.24. The 5-log reduction must hold for at least the product's shelf life under normal and moderate abuse storage. The 'pertinent microorganism' is the most resistant microorganism of public health significance likely to occur. Processors subject to Part 113/114, and those using a single thermal shelf-stability process (with the process in the hazard analysis), are exempt from 120.24(a). Citrus processors may use surface treatments after culling and cleaning within a single facility, with 120.25 E. coli verification testing.

explanation: 120.24(a) sets the standard: HACCP plan control measures that consistently achieve at least a 5-log reduction in the pertinent microorganism. 120.24 is the correct establishing section. J's two elements are supported. The exemptions and the citrus surface-treatment rule are useful qualifications but are not needed to answer what the standard is and which section sets it.

question_interpretation: Asks what postmarketing safety reporting requirements apply to a combination product applicant under 21 CFR Part 4, Subpart B.

issues.detail: G cites '4.100 through 4.110', but Subpart B ends at 4.105; there is no 4.106-4.110. The range should be 21 CFR 4.100-4.105, with 4.102 as the core section. The routing to Subpart B is correct.

J lists only the device-constituent reports (five-day, malfunction). For a combination product applicant, 4.102(c) also requires, depending on the constituent parts, correction/removal reports (806), field alert reports and fifteen-day reports for a drug constituent, and BPDRs and fifteen-day reports for a biological constituent. Fifteen-day reports are due in 30 calendar days if the product was authorized under a device application. J also leaves out 4.102(d) (periodic safety report summaries; additional reports on FDA request), 4.104 (submission manner) and 4.105 (recordkeeping).
Five-day and malfunction reports apply only if the combination product contains a device constituent part (4.102(c)(1)). J presents them as unconditional.

'Shared reporting responsibilities' is loosely put. 4.103 requires constituent part applicants to share death/serious-injury/adverse-experience information with the other constituent part applicant(s) within 5 calendar days and to keep records of it. The question is about a combination product applicant, which holds all the applications and so has no other constituent part applicant to share with.

explanation: The key points to the right subpart and gets the basic structure right: reporting depends on application type (4.102(b)) plus constituent-based reports (4.102(c)). But the citation range runs past the last existing section, and J covers only the device-constituent reports, presenting them as unconditional. J also misplaces the 4.103 sharing duty.
proposed_corrected_answer: A combination product applicant must (1) comply with the postmarketing safety reporting rules for its application type: Parts 803/806 for a device application, Part 314 for an NDA/ANDA, Parts 600/606 for a BLA (4.102(b)); and (2) also submit constituent-based reports (4.102(c)): for a device constituent, five-day reports, malfunction reports and correction/removal reports (with 806.20 records); for a drug constituent, field alert reports and fifteen-day reports; for a biological constituent, BPDRs and fifteen-day reports. Fifteen-day reports are due within 30 calendar days if the product was authorized under a device application. A report already submitted under 4.102(b) that meets the content, manner and deadline conditions need not be duplicated. Device-constituent report summaries go in periodic safety reports for NDA/ANDA/BLA products, and additional reports are required on FDA's written request for device-application products (4.102(d)). Reports are submitted per 4.104 and records kept for the longest applicable period (4.105). Where constituent parts are held by different applicants, each constituent part applicant must share death/serious injury/adverse experience information with the other(s) within 5 calendar days and keep records of it (4.103).
